title: "How many more of these kids do you want to see dead?": FW Mayor leads youth violence discussion - NewsBreak
text: FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WANE) — Mayor Sharon Tucker led a community discussion on Wednesday to address the recent uptick in youth violence in Fort Wayne. The discussion was held at the Allen County Public Library Main Branch and took place from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. Mayor Tucker was joined by Police Chief Scott Caudill, along with community advocates Roderick Parker of Big Hearts Community Projects and Foundation One of Unity Barber Shop. Andrew Downs, the city’s Director of Intergovernmental Affairs, moderated the discussion. “The panelists were chosen because of the work that they’ve done in the community,” says Mayor Tucker. “Foundation One has had boots on the ground for many, many years. Roderick was one of those kids 20 years ago, and so he, too, has lived experience on what it’s like to be a young person going through challenges.” The panel covered a variety of topics including ways to get kids out of situations that could become violent. Tucker pointed to offering teens jobs at the parks department or at Parkview Field to do something productive with their time. She also discussed a stricter curfew, but as the Fort Wayne Police Department has explained in the past , state law makes it difficult. Right now, Indianapolis is trying to lengthen its curfew, and the city is watching closely. “Right now we’re waiting to see how effective Indy’s is; it’s only been in place two or three weeks,” Caudill said. Parker also spoke on culture needing to change in order for kids to trust officers, noting that ight now those who participate in investigations may be labelled as “snitches.” Ultimately, Tucker said that she and the city staff are doing “everything we can” to combat youth violence, but several times doted on the fact that the city has limited resources to deal with the problem. They’re trying to get creative to find funds from federal sources and grants that wouldn’t drain the city’s coffers. “We’re looking at ways to work with our not-for-profits,” Tucker said. The theater was full of residents listening and taking in the discussion. All were adults in the crowd, but two young girls in high school and one recent South Side High School graduate. WANE 15 spoke with them and the Executive Director of Fort Wayne UNITED. “I think what the older adults need to start doing more is reach out to the youth,” said Ania Garcia, a South Side High School Graduate. “Instead of us having to come to them, have them come to us.” “There is a need in the community,” said George Hicks, Executive Director of Fort Wayne UNITED. “Whether it’s mental health, whether it’s understanding the needs of the family. Most of all, it’s just been able to connect with the young people. I think that was a great message tonight, is still understanding that we need to connect with the young people. One of the opportunities that was missed tonight is that the young people are not here.” While no definitive plan was made, meeting-goers were filled with hope that the discussion put the city in the right direction. “It’s simple,” says Roderick, “How many more of these kids do you want to see dead?” 190 spots were reserved for the public to attend and voice their concerns, ask questions, and share ideas on how to resolve the rise in violent crimes among area teens and young adults. “I read through all one hundred questions, two things that I received from that is, people want to know how they can help, and so we have a plan. I’m not going to give you that plan right now we will make that announcement in the future,” Tucker said. “People also want to know where they can get funding for their programs, and we have ideas on that as well.” The recorded discussion will be released for public viewing later in the week. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to WANE 15.
